stories.title: John Tanner: receiving, giving, and remembering
stories.introduction: John Tanner joined the Church in New York in 1832. Over the next eighteen years, his path led through Kirtland, Missouri, the Mississippi settlements, and the Salt Lake Valley. Along the way he gave money, endured violence and displacement, preached the gospel, and helped build two temples.

units.title: A hand offered in the name of Christ
paragraphs: John Tanner was a farmer and timberland owner in Bolton, New York, when missionaries brought him the restored gospel. He was fifty-four years old. Jared Carter recorded finding him unable to put weight on one foot after months of lameness. Tanner already believed in the Book of Mormon. Carter invited him to try walking in the name of Jesus Christ, took his hand, and commanded him to walk. In Carter’s account, Tanner was healed.

Tanner was baptized at Bolton Landing on September 17, 1832. The following February, Orson Pratt ordained him a priest. His new faith soon changed where he would live and what he would do with the property he had accumulated. The prosperous New York landowner began preparing to join the Saints in Ohio.

units.title: A decision that moved a household
paragraphs: In December 1834, Tanner felt an urgent need to go to Kirtland. He disposed of property and set out with his household on Christmas morning. The journey covered roughly five hundred miles. When the family arrived in January 1835, the Saints faced an immediate problem: money was due on the land where they were building the temple.

Tanner lent Joseph Smith $2,000 to meet that need. Joseph gave him a note for the loan. Tanner’s arrival connected a family’s long winter journey with the practical demands of a building already under construction.

units.title: Resources put to work at Kirtland
paragraphs: Tanner’s financial support extended beyond that first loan. He advanced funds to the temple committee and joined others in backing purchases of goods. These commitments put his own resources at risk. His name appears in the financial history of Kirtland as a lender, donor, and stockholder in the Kirtland Safety Society.

The temple was a shared undertaking. The revelation now recorded in Doctrine and Covenants 109 preserves Joseph Smith’s dedication prayer, offered on March 27, 1836. It speaks of the Saints’ poverty, their work, and their desire to build a house to God’s name. Tanner’s contributions helped meet material needs within that larger effort of worship and sacrifice.

units.title: A family within the gathering and displacement
paragraphs: Tanner left Kirtland for Far West in 1838. In Missouri, he was severely beaten during the violence against the Saints. By the following spring he had moved again, this time to New Liberty in Illinois. In March 1840 he settled near Montrose, across the Mississippi River from Nauvoo.

He again helped with temple construction, contributing to the Nauvoo Temple while rebuilding his family’s life. In April 1844, at sixty-five, he received a mission appointment to New York. The Church’s missionary record names David Pettegrew as his companion and records their departure on April 28. Tanner’s service now took him eastward again, away from the Mississippi settlements where he had made another home.

units.title: The note that became a remembered gift
paragraphs: Before that mission, according to the later family account, Tanner met Joseph Smith in Nauvoo and handed back the $2,000 note from Kirtland. Joseph asked what he wanted done with it. Tanner forgave the debt. A loan that had helped secure the temple land nearly a decade earlier became an outright gift.

After the Saints left Nauvoo, Tanner reached the Council Bluffs area in 1846. He and members of his family crossed the plains with the Willard Richards company in 1848; he was sixty-nine when that journey began. He settled in South Cottonwood in the Salt Lake Valley and died in 1850. The places in his record trace repeated departures and fresh beginnings, with his labor and means offered to the growing Church in each new home.

stories.title: Eleazer Miller: a simple witness and a continuing life
stories.introduction: Eleazer Miller is remembered for the testimony that helped Brigham Young accept the restored gospel. His life also included early missions in the northeastern United States and Canada, a family journey across the plains, and many years in Utah.

units.title: A listener who wanted to know
paragraphs: Brigham Young encountered the Book of Mormon soon after its publication in 1830. Copies reached his family through the missionary work of Samuel Smith. Brigham examined the message for about two years before accepting baptism. He was a working craftsman in Mendon, New York, making and repairing furniture and fitting doors, windows, and other woodwork.

At home, his wife Miriam was ill with tuberculosis. Alongside earning a living, Brigham helped care for her and their two young daughters. His search for religious truth unfolded within those daily responsibilities. He read, listened, and considered what the missionaries taught before committing himself to the Church.

units.title: A missionary before the famous encounter
paragraphs: Eleazer Miller was born in Coeymans, New York, in 1795. He married Rebecca Van Zant in 1816. The Church’s biographical database dates his baptism to May 1831 and records missionary service in New York and Pennsylvania that year, followed by another New York mission in 1832. In the spring of 1832 he was thirty-six; Brigham was thirty.

Miller carried his new faith beyond his own household. His recorded assignments would also take him to the Earnestown and Loughborough area of Upper Canada from June through September 1832. His encounter with Brigham belonged to this early period of preaching, when converts were already taking the message to other communities.

units.title: What Brigham remembered hearing
paragraphs: Brigham later described hearing a man who lacked polished speech or conspicuous learning bear a simple testimony of the Book of Mormon and Joseph Smith’s prophetic calling. Church teaching materials identify that missionary as Eleazer Miller. What stayed with Brigham was the conviction with which the witness was offered and the spiritual confirmation he himself experienced.

In his recollection, the Holy Ghost illuminated his understanding. He became convinced that the testimony was true. Miller’s words reached a man who had already spent a long time examining the gospel. The remembered encounter joins those two parts of Brigham’s conversion: patient inquiry and a personal witness of the Spirit.

units.title: An outward covenant in April 1832
paragraphs: On a cold, snowy day in April 1832, Miller baptized Brigham in Brigham’s own millstream. Brigham later remembered feeling humble and childlike, with an assurance that his sins were forgiven. He was confirmed and ordained an elder, and soon began preaching himself.

Miriam was baptized within a few weeks. Other members of the Young family and their neighbors also joined the growing Mendon branch. That September, Miriam died. Brigham’s first months in the Church held both the beginning of a new ministry and the loss of his wife, leaving him with their two daughters.

units.title: A life that continued westward
paragraphs: Sixteen years later, Miller and Rebecca traveled west in Brigham Young’s 1848 company. Miller was fifty-two. John Heward, writing about his own journey, remembered starting west in company with Miller and spending several days at Winter Quarters before moving onward. Heward described the larger journey’s practical demands: finding feed, using buffalo chips for fuel, caring for footsore cattle, and receiving help with teams as the travelers approached the mountains.

The company reached the Salt Lake Valley in September. Miller’s record continued in Utah long after the millstream baptism for which he became best known. He died in Salt Lake City on April 12, 1876, aged eighty. His service had stretched from the small branches of the early 1830s to the established communities of the American West.

stories.title: John Rowe Moyle: the stonecutter and the wooden leg
stories.introduction: John Rowe Moyle brought his family from England in 1856 and settled in Alpine, Utah. A skilled stonecutter, he traveled to Salt Lake City to work on the temple. After losing a leg, he fashioned a wooden replacement and eventually returned to the work.

units.title: A family on the road in 1856
paragraphs: John Rowe Moyle and his wife joined the Church in England in 1851. Five years later, they emigrated with their children. Moyle was forty-eight when the family joined Edmund Ellsworth’s handcart company for the overland journey to Utah.

His own brief journal records the earlier rail journey from Boston to Iowa, arriving on June 2. After about a week in camp, he left with the first handcart division under Ellsworth. The company’s route continued from Iowa City across the plains, reaching Salt Lake City on September 26, 1856. The rail trip, camp preparations, and months on the trail were successive stages of the family’s move to a new home.

units.title: A skill offered to a shared undertaking
paragraphs: The Moyles settled in Alpine, south of Salt Lake City. Their home and farm were there, while the temple site lay about twenty-two miles away. Moyle was an accomplished stonecutter, and his skill was wanted for the temple. He undertook the journey on foot, leaving the family’s horse available for work at home.
His stone house survives at the historic Moyle property, now an Alpine city park. The home preserves the setting of the family life and farm work that continued alongside his temple service.

units.title: The distance between home and the work
paragraphs: The weekly journey began before daylight. In the account retold by Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Moyle left home at about two o’clock on Monday morning to reach work by eight. He stayed in Salt Lake City during the week. After work ended on Friday evening, he walked home again, arriving around midnight.
During those working weeks he lodged with a son in Salt Lake City. Friday’s return took him back to the farm and family in Alpine; Monday brought the long outward journey again.

units.title: Making a way to walk again
paragraphs: An injury eventually cost Moyle a leg. During his recovery, he made a wooden replacement with an articulated ankle and foot. He practiced walking on it, gradually rebuilding the endurance needed for the journey to Salt Lake City. Uchtdorf’s account describes pain and persistence as he learned to use it.
A wooden leg associated with Moyle survives in the Daughters of Utah Pioneers museum collection. It is a tangible reminder of the adaptation that enabled this stonecutter to resume his working life.

units.title: Remembering the worker beyond the obstacle
paragraphs: Moyle returned to temple work. He is remembered for carving the dedicatory inscription on the east side of the Salt Lake Temple. The words named the purpose of the building he had helped shape over years of skilled labor: holiness to the Lord and a house of the Lord.

He died on February 15, 1889, before the completed temple was dedicated in April 1893. His story therefore ends before the great dedication gathering. The finished building carried forward work he had already given—through the long journeys from Alpine, the loss of his leg, the making of a replacement, and his return to the stone.
